text: Fault-tolerant quantum computers that can run serious algorithms don't exist yet — but the decision of whether an algorithm is even worth pursuing on one can't wait for them to exist. The Azure Quantum Resource Estimator is Microsoft's answer: a free, first-class service that answers what this would actually cost, years before the hardware to run it is built.

Four things to know. It is not a simulator — it doesn't execute your program to get a result. The inputs are your compiled Q# program plus configurable hardware assumptions: physical qubit technology, target logical error rate, error-correction code parameters. The outputs are physical qubit counts and runtime projections, a structured report rather than measurement results. And there's no direct equivalent integrated into the core Qiskit toolchain — this is a genuinely distinctive, free, push-button Azure Quantum feature.

Here's the real shape of the service, from Microsoft's own documentation: your application — the compiled Q# program — and an architecture model describing the hardware assumptions both feed into the analysis, which can project results across a Pareto frontier of different hardware tradeoffs, rather than handing back just one number.

To make this concrete, here's a deliberately simplified illustrative calculation, not a real estimator output. A common simplified way to reason about surface-code error correction is that physical qubits needed per logical qubit scale roughly with the square of the code distance you choose. Picking an illustrative distance of fifteen gives roughly four hundred fifty physical qubits per logical qubit. For an illustrative algorithm needing six logical qubits, that's roughly twenty-seven hundred physical qubits total. This arithmetic is verified and consistent as stated — but the real service runs a far more detailed analysis against your specific program and chosen qubit parameters.

Why run the same program through the estimator multiple times? Because changing the qubit-parameter assumptions and re-running is the entire point — it lets you ask how much a better physical qubit, or a different error-correction code, would actually save you, without needing that better qubit to exist yet.

Next lesson ties the resource estimator back into the same job lifecycle as every other target in this chapter: submit, poll, retrieve — the same shape whether you're running a simulator, the estimator, or real hardware.
